1:
The unnamed feast is the first thing every witness argues about, and the answers cover almost the whole calendar. puritan-evangelical Henry takes it flatly for the passover, since that was the most celebrated feast, and wesleyan-arminian Clarke reports the same as the judgement of the best critics, noting that several excellent manuscripts add the article and so read the feast, the grand and principal festival. reformed Gill canvasses Pentecost and tabernacles before settling on the passover, on the ground that this evangelist is very particular in accounting for the passovers of Christ’s ministry. Lightfoot builds the same case from the shape of the Gospel: the other evangelists mention no passover between the baptism and the death except the last, while this one points at them all, and this is the second. Calvin, however, argues for Pentecost from the itinerary — Christ left Jerusalem after the passover, passed through Samaria, healed the courtier’s son in Galilee, and only then came up to this feast — so that the order of time leads to Pentecost, though he declines to dispute the point. Wesley gives the same answer in two words, and the Latin catena assumes it.

grammatical-historical Ellicott dissents from all of these. There is, he says, perhaps no Jewish feast with which this one has not been identified, and one scholar has even proclaimed it the Day of Atonement; but the better reading omits the article, and the time-limits are fixed by the four months named earlier in the Gospel and by the passover named later, an interval falling in an intercalary year with a second month of Adar. The only feast inside that interval is Purim, kept on the fourteenth of Adar in memory of the deliverance from Haman and named from the lots he cast — one of the most popular feasts, marked by festive rejoicing, presents and gifts to the poor — and with this, Ellicott holds, the best modern opinion identifies the feast of the text. Barnes and Robertson decline to decide. Barnes says it may have been the passover, or Pentecost, or tabernacles, since all three required the attendance of the males, and that it is of no consequence which. Robertson adds that the opening phrase is one this evangelist uses vaguely, that it does not mean the incident follows immediately, and that there may well have been a passover not named among the three he does record.

On why Christ went up at all the witnesses agree more nearly. Henry gives two reasons: it was an ordinance of God which, as a subject made under the law, he would observe, though as a Son he might have pleaded exemption — and by this he teaches us to attend religious assemblies; and it was an opportunity of good, since great numbers were gathered from all parts of the country besides proselytes from abroad, and since a mind inclined to devotion and given over to the exercises of piety lies open to further discoveries of divine light and love. Calvin says the same in his own order: partly because the great multitude gave him the opportunity of publishing his doctrine more widely, and partly because it was necessary that he should be subject to the law in order to redeem us from its bondage. Among the latin-fathers, Augustine puts the first of those reasons as a matter of reputation — he always went up at the feasts so that it might be seen he was no enemy to the law but an observer of it — and adds that the crowds drawn in from the neighbouring towns gave him occasion to impress the simple multitude by miracles and teaching. Robertson notes only that the ascent to Jerusalem was upward from every direction save one.
2:
Four witnesses correct the same word. reformed Gill points out that market is not in the text, that no such market is described in Scripture or in the Jewish writings, and that sheep and oxen were in any case sold in the temple; what is meant is the sheep gate, through which the animals were brought into the city. grammatical-historical Barnes says the same and notes that the gate is repeatedly named in the record of the rebuilt walls, and that since the beasts were brought mainly for sacrifice it must have stood near the temple. Robertson simply supplies the noun from the same source. Ellicott finds the Vulgate’s alternative tempting, which takes the adjective with pool and gives a sheep-pool, but rules it out because the Greek word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and only in those passages of the Old.

Where the pool stood, and what its name meant, they answer with less confidence. Ellicott observes that the gate was well enough known to fix the locality but is itself now unknown, that the traditional identification with the gate named for Stephen fails because that gate did not exist until the time of Agrippa, and that the site long pointed out near the fortress of Antonia has been abandoned since a modern authority preferred an intermittent spring. Robertson notes that twin pools were found north of the temple late in the last century. On the name, Barnes, Ellicott and wesleyan-arminian Wesley agree on house of mercy, Barnes deriving it from the healing properties, while Robertson lists the manuscript rivals, one reading house of the olive. Calvin sets aside a fanciful reading proposed by an ancient scholar and offers his own: the water was carried in by conduits so that the priests could draw from it, or the name arose from its being poured in through pipes, the pool being so called because the beasts to be sacrificed were washed there.

The present tense of there is raises a question of date. Wesley takes it to show that this Gospel was written before Jerusalem was destroyed, about thirty years after the ascension. Clarke doubts it: Jerusalem had certainly fallen many years before this Gospel was written, though that need not mean the pool fell with it, and something in its place is still shown to travellers. He adds that the Syriac, Arabic, Persic and Armenian all read was, which he takes as proof that the pool no longer existed when those versions were made and that what is shown now is not the original. Robertson knows the argument for an early date and answers that the present tense is probably only the evangelist’s vivid memory.

Two smaller points fill out the scene. Lightfoot explains that in the Hebrew tongue means the language of those beyond the Euphrates, the Chaldee that had been the nation’s mother tongue since the return from Babylon, so named to distinguish it from the ancient holy tongue used before the captivity; those to whom it was native were called Hebrews, as distinct from the Hellenists. Ellicott and Robertson say the same more briefly, that what is meant is the current Aramaic. As for the word rendered pool, Barnes allows a pond, a fish-pool, or any water collected for bathing; Robertson calls it a swimming pool occurring only here in the New Testament; Clarke reports a bishop’s judgement that it should be rendered bath, the place being built for bathing. Wesley guesses the basin had five sides to match its porticoes, which he takes to have been built for the sick; Robertson explains the word as a covered colonnade. Calvin draws the point of the whole description: the crowds that resorted there, and the nearness of the temple, show that the miracle to come was neither concealed nor known to a few.
3:
A textual question governs the passage. grammatical-historical Ellicott reports that the clause about waiting for the moving of the water and the whole of the following verse are omitted by most of the oldest manuscripts, including the two great fourth-century codices, and judged no part of the original text by a consensus of modern editors. He finds it interesting that a gloss should have made its way in and be now regarded by ninety-nine readers in every hundred as integral to the Gospel; Robertson agrees, calling the addition Western and Syrian and made to throw light on the word troubled, and remarks that it is a relief to many to know the verse is spurious. wesleyan-arminian Clarke stands against them: the clause and the verse are wanting in some manuscripts, but he thinks the evidence against their authenticity insufficient, and notes that the leading critic of his day, though marking the passage doubtful, left it in the text.

The angel divides them further. Clarke reports the attempt to naturalise the account — that the healing virtue came from washing the entrails of the sacrifices in the water, and the angel was only a man sent to stir up the sediment, which then penetrated the bather’s pores — and calls it a miserable shift to get rid of the power and goodness of God, as unlikely as it is insupportable. He adds that many authorities read an angel of the Lord, which if genuine destroys the conjecture, and that those who feel little of the work of God in their own hearts are unwilling to allow it in others. reformed Gill rejects the same conjecture, allowing only that the angel may have come visibly or been inferred by the people from the unusual agitation of the water.

Barnes takes the opposite line without abandoning the angel. It is not affirmed that anyone saw him; they judged by the effect, the Jews being in the habit of attributing every favour to angelic ministry. The fountain, he holds, had strong medicinal properties like other famous waters that heal what is otherwise incurable, and nothing miraculous appears in it beyond this, that its periodical agitation was produced by an angel. Robertson goes further: the Jews explained an intermittent spring by angelic ministry, but the periodicity of such visits makes it hard to believe. Wesley acknowledges that many thought the thing purely natural, guesses that the descent came at a certain hour during the paschal week, and notes that the Greek implies the angel had ceased going down before the Gospel was written. He reads a purpose in it: to raise expectation of the approaching acceptable time, to add lustre to the Son’s miracles, and to show that the ancient people were not forgotten — for one was healed here, where the Son of God healed multitudes daily.

Calvin turns the angel into a warning. Curing the sick was a work peculiar to God, but as he was accustomed to employ the ministry of angels he charged them with this duty; they are called powers not because God gives up his office and sits unemployed in heaven, but because by acting powerfully in them he displays his own power. It is therefore wicked to make them the medium between us and God, as though God stood at a distance when in fact he uses them as manifestations of his presence: we must come direct to Christ, under whose guidance the angels become assistants of our salvation. Lightfoot supplies a limit: it is hardly imaginable that the sick lay there day and night the year round, so the troubling was probably confined to the solemn feasts. Gill reads the crowd as an emblem of men under the law of works, unable to keep it or to atone for breaking it; Barnes explains impotent as feeble from long disease rather than acutely ill.
5:
grammatical-historical Ellicott is precise about the number: the thirty-eight years measure neither the man’s age nor his time at the pool but the duration of the infirmity, so that he had spent half the ordinary lot of human life in that condition. Helpless and friendless, he appeals without an uttered word to the Mercy that is present in the House of Mercy; and Ellicott notes that of all whom Christ healed this man alone is addressed first, unasked. Robertson gives the phrase literally — having spent thirty and eight years. Barnes admits we do not know what the disease was, only that it disabled him from walking, was of very long standing, and was doubtless reckoned incurable. wesleyan-arminian Clarke records an ancient conjecture that the infirmity was blindness, prefers a palsy, and dwells on how deplorable the case was, with poverty and disease joined: unable to reach the pool himself and with no one to help him. He also turns the length of the affliction into evidence, since a condition of thirty-eight years must have been known to multitudes, so that the man could not have been someone prepared for the occasion; all Christ’s miracles, he adds, were wrought on such persons and occasions as to preclude any possibility of imposture.

reformed Calvin reads the same details the same way. The evangelist is collecting circumstances that prove the miracle certain: the long duration had removed all hope of cure, the man was deprived of the very remedy at hand, and there was nobody to help him — all of which makes the power of Christ more strikingly displayed. When a man rises suddenly whole and strong in every limb that had been useless, so sudden a change is the more fitted to strike the minds of those who saw it. Gill fixes the scene, in one of the five porches beside the pool.

Why Christ asked a question at all divides the witnesses. Lightfoot answers that there was no doubt about the man’s wish, since he had lain there so long for that very purpose, and that the question really has respect to the day: it amounts to asking whether he would be healed on the sabbath, the nation being infinitely superstitious in that matter. Clarke takes it as pastoral technique — Christ meant to excite faith, hope and a greater desire of being healed, wishing the man to reflect on his misery so as to be better prepared to receive a cure and to value it when it came — and adds that addresses of this kind are always proper from preachers of the gospel, since such questions are often put to the soul by the Spirit of God. Calvin allows a double purpose: partly to kindle in the man a desire for the favour offered, partly to quicken the attention of the bystanders, who in a sudden occurrence might otherwise have missed the miracle altogether. Ellicott and Robertson both put the weight on the verb, which asks not whether he expects healing but whether he wills it; Robertson adds that we are not told how Jesus knew the man’s history, whether by supernatural knowledge, by observation, or by overhearing what people said, and calls the question pertinent and sympathetic.

eastern-antiochene John Chrysostom takes the scene as an argument for reading Scripture at all. The divine oracles, he says, are a treasury of every kind of medicine: whether one needs to quench pride, to lull desire to sleep, to tread underfoot the love of money, to despise pain, to gain confidence or to learn patience, abundant resource is there. What man struggling with long poverty, or nailed to a grievous disease, will not take much comfort from this passage? For here is a man paralytic for thirty-eight years, watching others delivered every year while he remained bound, and not even so giving way.
7:
grammatical-historical Barnes says the reply implies the man did wish to be healed, but that on top of every other trial he had no friend. wesleyan-arminian Wesley says the same in a line: he gives the reason why he was not made whole notwithstanding his desire. Clarke notes that several manuscripts begin the reply with an explicit yes — yea, Lord, but I have no man — and turns to the reader: when long affliction is allied to deep poverty, the state is deplorable. reformed Gill observes that the address was a common courteous form. Robertson explains the belief behind the complaint: at each outflow of the intermittent spring the healing power belonged to the first one in, so the request is to be thrown in before anyone else. Ellicott dwells on the helplessness: there is an eloquence in it more powerful than words. Day by day the man had listened for the first sound, summoned the feeble vestiges of his strength for the one action on which everything depended, and hoped again in spite of despair — and always another went down before him. That, he adds, is the unspoken cry of thousands still.

Calvin makes the reply a mirror. The man does what almost all of us do, limiting the assistance of God to his own conception of it; Christ forgives the weakness, as he daily forgives ours, when we fix our attention on the means within reach and he meanwhile puts out his hand from hidden places, showing how far his goodness goes beyond the narrow limits of our faith. It teaches patience too, thirty-eight years being a long delay for a favour God had determined from the beginning to confer.

On the command Clarke says Christ speaks as God, in no name but his own and with an authority belonging to God alone. He notes a habit: after a miracle Christ attached some circumstance attesting its truth — the fragments gathered after the loaves, the steward made to taste the wine, the lepers sent to the priests — and the carried bed is one such. Barnes agrees the bed was carried as proof of the cure, and draws the lesson that when Jesus gives a command he can also give strength to obey it. Robertson hears the first imperative as an exclamation and notes the two verbs differ, one telling him to pick up the pallet at once and the other to go on walking. Ellicott raises the difficulty that no demand for faith precedes the healing, and answers that if faith is a living principle rather than a form of words, no more striking instance could be sought than this man; Christ sees that receptive power, which in his helplessness is strength, and calls it out.

Lightfoot supplies the rule that makes the command dangerous: nothing might be carried on the sabbath from a private place into a public one or the reverse, the offence bringing a sin offering if unadvised and stoning if presumptuous. Barnes and Clarke both list why the command was right: the Son of man was Lord of the sabbath, the man was poor and was told to secure his property, and the Jews had stretched the day’s obligation beyond its intention, so that Christ took every opportunity to restore it to its proper use. Clarke adds that a public monument of God’s power was not contrary to the spirit of a day made to honour him. Calvin knows how much offence would follow and says Christ chose the exhibition deliberately, that the miracle might be more widely known and open the way for the discourse that follows; from which he draws a rule, that though the whole world kindle into rage we are to proclaim the glory of God so far as his glory requires. Robertson marks the moment as the first of the sabbath collisions in Jerusalem.
10:
grammatical-historical Ellicott catches the moral of the scene in a sentence: what they cannot deny, they can cavil at. One might have expected wonder and thankfulness that the man could walk at all; what comes instead is the murmur of a formalism that had bound the letter round men until it had well-nigh crushed all heart out of them. He notes that the bearing of burdens was specially forbidden by the prophet, and that the rabbis pressed the prohibition to cover a burden of any kind. Robertson says the same from the wording: the objection quotes back the very words Jesus had used, carrying was reckoned unlawful, stoning was the rabbinical penalty, and the healing of the man was treated as a minor detail. grammatical-historical Barnes adds only that the Jews supposed the prohibition to stand in the Old Testament and were very strenuous in the external duties of religion. reformed Gill fixes the moment, when they saw him either at the pool or walking through the streets with his bed on his back.

Calvin declines to make the objection simple bigotry. It was the duty of all to maintain the sanctity of the sabbath, he says, and on that footing they justly and properly accuse the man; their fault begins only when his excuse fails to satisfy them, since once the reason was known he ought to have been acquitted. Carrying a burden was indeed a violation, but Christ, who laid the burden on his shoulders, discharges him by his own authority. From this Calvin draws a rule of judgement: whatever contradicts the word of God deserves to be condemned without hesitation, yet because mistakes so frequently happen in this matter we ought first to inquire modestly and calmly, so that our decision may be sound and sober. The Jews, prejudiced by wicked dispositions, had no patience to inquire, and so shut the door against judgement and moderation altogether.

The healed man’s reply is defended by every witness. Barnes says he reasoned correctly: if Jesus had power to work so signal a miracle he had a right to explain the law, and if he had conferred so great a favour he had a right to expect obedience — from which Barnes draws the wider conclusion that the mercy of God in pardoning sin lays on us the same obligation, whatever the men of the world may think of us. wesleyan-arminian Clarke sets out the same argument as a syllogism: one who could work such a miracle must be at least the best of men, and a good man will neither do evil himself nor command it in others, so there could be no evil in carrying the bed. Ellicott puts it more simply still — the man rests the use of the power on the will of the one who gave it, since that has been the single divine voice he has heard, and it cannot be wrong to obey it. Robertson notes the emphatic demonstrative with which he points at his healer, and the fact that he did not know who Jesus was or even his name, but could only repeat his words.
12:
grammatical-historical Barnes finds in the question a remarkable instance of the perverseness of men and of their want of candour. Instead of looking at the miracle, or at the man’s account of how it was done, they look only at what they took for a breach of the law; they assumed that nothing could make the carrying of a bed proper, and meditated vengeance not merely on the man but on whoever told him to do it. One great source of dispute among men, Barnes adds, is that they look only at the points on which they differ and will not listen to the reasons for the difference. Ellicott sharpens the same observation: they pass over the giving of the power altogether and quote only the command that falls under their technical prohibition, so that the life and strength of once-palsied limbs count for nothing. The real motive, he holds, is a charge against the one whose power the body of the people was feeling as a life-current, quickening deadened energies and rousing men to a sense of God’s presence among them; men and women who had lain all their lives in moral helplessness, never helped by their own priests and rulers, were now standing in the strength their new Teacher gave, and it could not be denied. Robertson hears contempt in the phrasing — who is the fellow? — and notes that they ask about the command and not about the cure. reformed Gill says they were already suspecting who had done it.

That the man could not tell them is variously explained. Gill supposes he had never seen and perhaps never even heard of Christ before, and that Christ gave him no opportunity to converse or so much as ask who he was. Barnes says the healer had silently mingled with the crowd and passed on unobserved, and that the man had been so overjoyed at his cure that he never inquired the name of his benefactor. wesleyan-arminian Clarke reads the verb as a withdrawal easily made in a crowd, notes the suggestion that Christ withdrew on seeing a multitude gathering into a tumult over the carried bed, and adds that he had not yet finished his work and would not expose himself to the envy and malice of the rulers. Robertson explains the rare verb, which may mean to swim out, to slip away, or to turn the head aside, and takes the crowd as the stated reason for the departure.

Ellicott resists that last reading. The marginal rendering shows the translators did not mean that a crowd had gathered round the miracle and that Christ left to avoid it — for in that case the man must have known who he was — though the English probably conveys as much to most readers. Better, he says, to render it freely: Jesus disappeared among the multitude which was in the place. The crowd is not given as the reason for his going, but as the explanation of how he passed on unrecognised after speaking. Calvin agrees on the effect and gives a further purpose: Christ did not mean the glory of so great a work to be lost, but meant it to become generally known before he owned himself its author, so he withdrew a little that the Jews might judge the fact itself without reference to any person. Calvin then draws a hard conclusion. The cure cannot be ascribed to the man’s faith, since even after being made whole he does not acknowledge his Physician; and though he carried his bed when ordered, which looks like the guidance of faith, and though Calvin does not deny some secret movement of it in him, what follows shows he had no solid doctrine or clear light on which to rely.
14:
reformed Gill supposes the man went straight from home to the temple, to show himself, attend the worship and give thanks. grammatical-historical Barnes adds that those raised from a bed of sickness should seek the sanctuary and thank God, since nothing is more improper than to forget our benefactor. wesleyan-arminian Clarke turns it round: how many, when made well, forget the hand that healed them and use their renewed strength in the service of sin — a use of God’s mercies that makes the restoration a respite only from perdition. Ellicott finds no mark of time but thinks it was probably the same day, the first use of the restored power being to bring a thank-offering. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom makes the point sharply: the healed man did not go to the market place or give himself to pleasure or vainglory, but — a great mark of religion — went to the temple; and where he had not recognised his healer in the crowd, in a sacred place he does.

The warning that follows is read by most as a diagnosis. Barnes says it implies that the infirmity was caused by sin, perhaps by vice in the man’s youth, and that Christ shows he knew the cause. Robertson renders it no longer go on sinning and calls it a clear implication that this disease was due to personal sin, as so often; not all sickness is, he adds, but much of it is, and nature is a hard paymaster. Wesley says only that the former illness seems to have been the effect or punishment of sin. Ellicott presses the tense: the present imperative points not to a single act but to a permanent condition, be not any more a sinner; the man has been freed from the effects, and if they were truly remedial, from the cause too. Clarke notes Christ was giving proof of the perfection of his knowledge, since he knew the secret of the past.

John Chrysostom generalises the principle behind it. Sin is a fearful thing and the ruin of the soul, and its mischief has often overflowed and attacked men’s bodies as well; for when the soul is diseased we feel no pain, while for a small hurt to the body we use every exertion, and so God often punishes the body for the transgressions of the soul, that by the scourging of the inferior part the better part may receive some healing. He compares the apostle checking a soul’s disease by the destruction of the flesh, as a physician applies external cautery when internal remedies fail. On the closing threat, Ellicott observes that there is then something worse than a life of unmoving helplessness, and hears sadness even in behold, thou art made whole: there are men for whom it had been good never to have been born, and limbs that had better never have moved. Robertson makes the same comparison plainly — worse than thirty-eight years of illness, bad as that is — because from now on the man will be sinning against knowledge.

Calvin declines the diagnostic reading and takes the verse for gratitude. The reappearance shows that when Christ concealed himself it was never so the memory of the kindness should perish; he meant the work to be known first and himself acknowledged as its Author afterwards, and now comes forward of his own accord. The doctrine of the passage is that we make an improper use of the gifts of God if we are not stirred by them to thankfulness. Christ does not reproach the man with what he had given him, but reminds him that he was cured in order that, remembering the favour, he might serve God his Deliverer all his life; for as God by stripes instructs and spurs us to repentance, so by his goodness and forbearance he invites us to it.
15:
grammatical-historical Ellicott says we are not told why the man reported his healer, but that it was natural to give the answer he could not give before, and to secure himself against the charge by naming his authority. The narrative does not suggest defiance, still less that he used his new strength to lay a charge against the giver of it; the impression is rather that he took the power to have come from a prophet and told God’s representatives, supposing they would recognise him too. reformed Calvin agrees: nothing was further from his intention than to make Christ an object of hatred, or from his expectation than that they would rage so furiously; his intention was pious, to render his Physician the honour justly due. Gill adds that he left not in resentment but delighted at having found his benefactor. wesleyan-arminian Clarke notes the exact form of the report: he did not say Jesus had ordered him to carry his bed, only that Jesus had cured him, and left them to draw the inference.

Robertson alone reads it darkly. Instead of heeding the warning about his own sins, the man went off and told the Jews, to clear himself with the ecclesiastics and escape a possible stoning; he was either ungrateful and wilfully betrayed Jesus, or incompetent and did not see that he was bringing trouble on his benefactor, and in either case one has small respect for him. Wesley turns from the man to the result. One might have expected that when such a benefactor was named, crowds would have thronged to hear him; instead they surround him with hostile intent and conspire against his life, and for an imagined transgression in a point of ceremony would have put out this light of Israel. Let us not wonder, then, if our own good is evil spoken of.

Barnes catalogues the injustice. They opposed him, attempted to ruin his character, and held him up as a violator of the law; instead of asking whether he had given proof of being the Messiah, they assumed he must be wrong and ought to be punished, which is what every bigot does with those who differ from him. All he had done was to restore an infirm man — a thing they would have done for their cattle. Gill notes the persecution was at first with the tongue, reviling him as a sabbath-breaker and a destroyer of the law. Robertson hears an inceptive tense, began to persecute and kept it up: they had disliked him at his first visit and were suspicious of his popularity, and now they had cause for an open breach.

A textual question closes the verse. Ellicott holds that the words about seeking to slay him should be omitted, having been inserted in some manuscripts to explain the opening of the verse that follows; and he presses the imperfect in the other clause, he was doing these things, expressing custom: either they generalised a rule of practice from this single instance, or some earlier unrecorded miracles had also been worked on a sabbath. Robertson reads the same tense the same way, that Jesus was becoming a regular sabbath-breaker in their eyes. Clarke reports that the clause is missing from several manuscripts and versions, and that the leading critic of his day left it out — but he does not think it should go, and observes that it was true of them whether the evangelist wrote it or not. He adds that the spirit of religious persecution has always been the most fell and dangerous disposition on this side of perdition, since every other has some moderator while this one is wholly abandoned to its guide.
17:
The defence is a single sentence, and the witnesses agree that it moves the argument to entirely new ground. puritan-evangelical Henry notes that on other occasions Christ had pleaded lower precedents — David eating the shewbread, the priests slaying the sacrifices, the people watering their cattle — but that here he waives every such plea and alleges the example of his Father and his own divine authority, insisting on the one argument that is equivalent to all the rest. reformed Gill sets the scene, Christ convened before them and charged, and answering in his own vindication.

grammatical-historical Barnes unfolds the premise: God has not ceased to work on the sabbath, but makes the sun rise, rolls the stars, and causes the grass and the tree and the flower to grow. He finished the work of creation in six days and rested from that, but he has never suspended his government of the world or the carrying forward of his purposes, so the obligation to rest does not extend to him. As God does good on that day and is not bound by the law that binds his creatures, so, Christ says, do I. Clarke says the same and draws the sharper conclusion: since nothing could continue to exist without the continual energy of God, in this respect he can keep no sabbaths — and to the Son, constantly employed in governing and supporting all things, comforting the wretched and saving the lost, there is in this respect no sabbath either. Ellicott finds the premise a commonplace of the age, quoting a contemporary Jewish philosopher for whom working is the property of God as burning is the property of fire; the rest of the seventh day completed the works of creation but was never a cessation of divine energy, which knows neither day nor night, nor summer nor winter, nor sabbath nor jubilee. Robertson notes the same fact was pointed out by that philosopher and by the early Christian writers, that the possessive is my and not our Father, and that Christ made the sabbath for man’s blessing but cannot keep it himself.

Calvin is careful about what the defence does not say. Christ does not answer that the law of the sabbath was temporary and now due to be abolished — though Calvin grants elsewhere that the ceremony was one of the shadows of the law, ended by his coming — because the present question does not turn on that. Men are commanded to abstain from their own works only, which is why circumcision, being a work of God and not of men, was never held at variance with the sabbath. What Christ insists on is that the holy rest enjoined by the law is not disturbed when we are employed in the works of God. wesleyan-arminian Wesley states the proposition baldly — from the creation until now the Father has worked without intermission, and I do likewise — and observes that everything following in the chapter is the explanation and defence of it.

Lightfoot reads the answer as two claims made at once before the council: that the Messiah is God, and that Christ is the Messiah. Son of God and Messiah, he says, are convertible terms which the Jews do not deny, though their conceptions of what sonship means are very wrong; the confession of Peter and the question of the high priest both pair the titles, yet the parties hardly agree on the sense. He then surveys the rabbinic dispute — one commentator granting that the psalm which bids men kiss the Son speaks properly of the Messiah, while another discussion argues vehemently against any true filiation, and the figure in the fiery furnace who is like a son of God is taken by some for an angel.
18:
Every witness holds that the hearers understood exactly what had been claimed. wesleyan-arminian Clarke says they took no wrong meaning out of the words, since Christ had plainly stated that whatever was the Father’s work was his also, and so showed that he and the Father were one; they now had two pretences for taking his life, that he had dissolved the obligation of the sabbath and that he was guilty of blasphemy in making himself equal with God, either of which the law punished with death. Wesley presses the possessive: the Greek means his own Father in a sense in which no creature could speak, and it is evident that all the hearers so understood him, and that our Lord never contradicted the inference but confirmed it. grammatical-historical Ellicott renders the clause his own Father for the same reason, noting that they recognise beyond doubt what the term means and what the attribute of ceaseless energy implies. It was a claim no one else had ever made, and they feel it to be a claim to divinity. Barnes draws the same conclusion from their reaction: their reading shows that in Jewish eyes calling God his Father implied equality with God.

Robertson traces the escalation. The imperfect gives a graphic picture of increased and untiring effort to be done with him, and the same clause recurs again and again later in the Gospel; their blood was up on the sabbath issue, and they bend every energy to it. He was now, in their eyes, a common and regular sabbath-breaker, the verb meaning to loosen or set at naught. The sabbath was the first grudge against him, but his defence had made the offence worse and handed them a far graver charge. reformed Gill says only that they were now the more resolute, and studied every way and means to bring it about.

Barnes turns the moment into a rule for preachers. The answer was fitted greatly to irritate them; Christ did not deny what he had done but added what he well knew would enrage them, and doubtless knew that it might endanger his life. From which Barnes draws three lessons: that we are not to keep back truth because it may endanger us; that we are not to keep it back because it will irritate and enrage sinners, since the fault is not in the truth but in the sinner; and that when one portion of truth enrages hypocrites they will only be enraged the more the longer they hear.

Calvin reaches the same practical point by another road. The defence was so far from allaying their fury that it enraged them further, and Christ was not unacquainted with their malignity and hardened obstinacy; he intended first to profit the few disciples then present, and then to make a public display of an incurable malice. By his example, Calvin says, he has taught us never to yield to the fury of wicked men but to maintain the truth of God as far as necessity demands, though the whole world should oppose and murmur; nor should the servants of Christ take it ill that they do not profit all men according to their wish, since Christ himself did not always succeed. We need not wonder, he adds, if in proportion as the glory of God is more fully displayed the adversary rages the more violently in his instruments. Calvin also notes that when the evangelist reports the charge of sabbath-breaking he is speaking according to the opinion the Jews had formed, the state of the case being in fact quite otherwise.
19:
The saying is a concession and a claim at once. reformed Gill notes that Christ neither denies the charge of blasphemy nor corrects any misreport of his words, but allows the whole and vindicates himself in so saying. Calvin puts it more strongly: he is so far from clearing himself that he maintains more openly that it is true, insisting the work they cavilled at was a divine work, so that if they persist in condemning it they must fight with God himself. latin-fathers Hilary reads the sentence as answering the sabbath charge and the jealousy together: what Christ did was in reality the Father’s doing, who acted in the Son, and this form of words asserts the excellency of his birth and nature while quieting the offence. Augustine of Hippo prefaces the discourse by observing what kind of Gospel this is: the evangelist who leaned on the Lord’s breast received the peculiar gift of uttering things which rouse the attentive minds of the little ones without filling them, while to minds of larger growth they give both exercise and food. What displeased the Jews here, he adds, pleased the Father.

The disputed question is whether the words concede inferiority. grammatical-historical Ellicott sets two errors side by side: the Jews saw equality with God in the claim and called it blasphemy, while men since have seen inferiority in it. The words Son and Father answer both. The essence of blasphemy is independence of God and rivalry with him, and Christ claims no such position, being as a Son subject to the Father’s will and morally unable to act of himself. wesleyan-arminian Clarke argues from the other end: any intelligent creature can do what God cannot, since it may err and may sin, so one who can do nothing but what God does is no creature at all — and the sabbath conclusion follows, that if he has broken it, so has God. Wesley calls the incapacity not an imperfection but a glory, resulting from an eternal and indissoluble unity, so that it is impossible for the Son to judge or will or testify or teach anything apart from the Father.

Calvin reports the ancient controversy and refuses both sides. Arius inferred that the Son is inferior; the orthodox fathers replied that the words mark nothing more than the distinction of person, so that Christ is from the Father yet not deprived of intrinsic power to act. Both, Calvin says, were wrong, since the discourse does not relate to the simple divinity of Christ. Barnes stays with the plain sense: of himself means nothing without the Father’s appointment and nothing contrary to him, the union being such that the Son can do nothing independently or without the Father’s concurrence. Robertson observes that the statement is in one sense true of every man but in a far deeper sense of Christ, and calls it a supreme example of a son copying the spirit and work of a father. Clarke adds that the reciprocity runs both ways, since neither can the Father act of himself, given his infinite unity with the Son.

Two witnesses take the sentence as a statement about office rather than nature. Lightfoot renders it as a maxim about the Messiah, a servant sent by his Father who must work not by his own will but his sender’s; the Jew, however he may try to elude the phrase Son of God, cannot deny that maxim, and expounds it himself not of weakness but of the perfection and obedience of the Son. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem says Christ made all things — angels, dominions, thrones — not because the Father wanted strength to create them, but because he willed that the Son should reign over his own workmanship, giving him the design of what was to be made; and the Only-begotten speaks so in honouring his own Father.
20:
The ground of the last verse is now named as love. grammatical-historical Barnes traces the Son’s authority to that peculiar, ineffable and infinite love which God has for his only-begotten, feebly and dimly illustrated by the love an earthly parent bears an only child. Sheweth him he takes to mean makes him acquainted with, concealing nothing: from apostles, prophets and philosophers no small part of God’s doings is hidden, but from the Son nothing is; and since God shows him all that he does, the Son must be omniscient, for the whole range of God’s works could never be imparted to a finite mind. Ellicott builds the argument as a pair: as the relation of Son implies a moral inability to do anything apart from the Father, so the relation of Father implies a moral necessity to impart everything to the Son, and the unity of their work has the Eternal Love for its basis. Robertson notes that the verb for loving here is not the one used earlier in the Gospel — the one suggesting intimate friendship, the other deliberate choice — and that this evangelist uses both for the mystery of the Father’s love for the Son. reformed Gill grounds the love in what the Son is: his image, the brightness of his glory, of the same nature and equal to him.

Calvin dissents from the older exposition. That God loves himself in the Son is a harsh and far-fetched reading; the statement applies beautifully instead to Christ as clothed with flesh, and by this title he is distinguished from angels and from men. Christ was chosen so that the whole love of God might dwell in him and flow from him to us as from a full fountain, and he is loved by the Father as the Head of the church; the showing is to be understood as communication, the Father having given him his heart. Among the latin-fathers, Augustine of Hippo summarises what he had argued the day before: the works of Father and Son are inseparable, the Father doing all things through the Son as through his Word, by whom all things were made. He adds a rule for the hearer: it is better not to know than to go astray, and better to know than not to know, so that before all things we ought to strive to know.

What the greater works are is answered by anticipation. Barnes and wesleyan-arminian Clarke both point forward to the two named immediately after — the raising of the dead and the judgement of the world — against which the healing of an impotent man and the command to carry a bed are small. Ellicott takes them rather as belonging to the development of Christ’s human nature and mediatorial work, of which the works already done are but the first signs, and notes that the pronoun is emphatic: those who seek to kill him shall themselves see them. Robertson adds that there is more to follow even than that, since the disciples will in extent surpass what Christ is doing. Wesley observes that Christ oftener calls them works than signs or wonders, because they were no wonders in his eyes, and that the marvelling was literally fulfilled when he raised Lazarus; and he presses the simultaneity — at the same time, not at different times, the Father shows and does, and the Son sees and does.

Clarke closes with a caution about how the whole discourse is to be read. Our Lord sometimes speaks of himself as God and sometimes as the ambassador of God; since he had a human and a divine nature the distinction was essentially necessary, and many errors, Clarke says, have originated from want of attention to it.
21:
The greater works are now named, and latin-fathers Augustine states the case for them being greater: it is more of a miracle that a dead man should rise than that a sick man should recover. He then guards the sentence twice over. We are not to understand that some are raised by the Father and others by the Son, but that the Son raises to life the very same whom the Father raises; and lest anyone should say that the Father raises the dead through the Son, the one by his own power and the other as an instrument moved by another, Christ asserts the Son’s power distinctly — he quickens whom he will. Observe, says Augustine, not only the power but the will, for Father and Son have the same power and the same will.

grammatical-historical Barnes and wesleyan-arminian Clarke both begin from precedent. God has raised the dead before, in the son of the widow at Sarepta and the son of the Shunammite, and the Jews did not doubt it; but those raisings came by the ministry of prophets. Clarke presses the difference: Christ raises whom he pleases, as he did the ruler’s daughter, the widow’s son at Nain and Lazarus, giving life according to his own will and not obliged to supplicate for the power as the prophets were. Barnes draws the inference that since raising the dead must be among the highest attributes of divinity, and since Jesus claims to do it in the same manner as the Father, he must be equal with God. Robertson notes that so far as we know Jesus had not yet raised anyone, so that the claim runs ahead of the deed, with the widow’s son at Nain not far off; and he adds that the power reaches both body and soul.

How far the quickening is bodily is the question. reformed Gill allows both readings and leans to the spiritual, since the verb is a present — raiseth, not hath raised — so that the raising of dead sinners to a life of grace may be chiefly meant. Ellicott says the words are purposely general and that the following verses show the greater works to be resurrection and judgement, both of them spiritual as well as physical and present as well as future; the background is still the earlier saying, since resurrection and judgement are the Father’s work, while the manifestation of them within the limits of space and time is the Son’s. He notes that raising the dead and making alive are named as attributes of God throughout the older Scriptures. Calvin takes the widest view of all: though Christ appears to specify one class, this is a general doctrine in which he declares himself the Author of life, and life contains within itself not only righteousness but all the gifts of the Spirit and every part of our salvation. He also notices the pairing of the two verbs as deliberate, since Christ found us all dead and had therefore to begin with a raising, and it would not have been enough to be rescued from death if he did not fully and perfectly restore us.

Calvin adds that a miracle so remarkable was bound to yield this fruit, of opening a door for the gospel. Wesley maps what follows: the greater works are raising the dead and judging the world, and the power of quickening whom he will follows from the power of judging — the two being proposed here and in the next verse, and then taken up in order, the acquittal of believers, the quickening of some of the dead, and at last the general resurrection.
22:
reformed Gill reads the denial as elliptical: the Father judges no man without the Son, which proves their equality, for he certainly does judge — the old world, Sodom, Israel — but never apart from the Son. wesleyan-arminian Clarke and Wesley take it the same way, Clarke finding a confirmation that the Father acts not without the Son nor the Son without the Father, and Wesley adding that the Father judges by the man he has ordained. grammatical-historical Ellicott renders it more sharply — not even doth the Father judge any man — arguing that if not the Father, to whom judgement belongs, then none but the Son. He observes that judging is the opposite of quickening and the two powers correlative, the spiritual life given to some being itself a judgement of others. Barnes fixes on what the office requires: judging the world implies ability to search the heart and to understand all motives, which none but a divine being can do.

Calvin faces the objection head on. If the Father governs the world in the person of the Son, does he surrender his right to govern and sit unemployed in heaven like a private person? The answer is easy: no change took place in the Father when he appointed Christ supreme King, for he is in the Son and works in him; but because all our senses fail the moment we try to rise to God, Christ is set before our eyes instead. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem makes the same qualification: the Father does not divest himself of power but judges through the Son, and the Son judges by the Father’s will, the two wills being one and the same. Cyril then turns it on the hearer: let us dread lest God condemn us, who needs no proofs to condemn. Do not say you sinned in the night with no one by; you will be judged out of your own conscience, and will rise clothed either with your sins or with your righteous deeds.

The purpose clause turns the passage into a demand for worship. Clarke argues plainly: if the Son is honoured even as the Father, he must be God, receiving worship that belongs to God alone; and as worshipping any creature is idolatry, Christ is no creature, and if not a creature then the Creator. God, he adds, will not receive the adoration of the man who refuses that honour. Wesley adds a distinction: the honour will be paid either willingly, escaping condemnation by faith, or unwillingly, when the wrath of the Judge is felt. Were Christ God only by office and not in the unity of the divine essence, he could not be honoured with the very same honour. Robertson says Jesus claims the same right to worship that the Father has, and that there is small comfort here for those who praise him as a teacher while denying his claim to be worshipped.

Barnes defines the honour: to honour is to esteem, reverence and do homage, and we honour the Son when we regard him as possessed of wisdom, power and eternity equal with God. He supports it from outside the church: the earliest Christians were described in a Roman governor’s letter to his emperor as meeting to sing hymns to Christ as God. Calvin makes the clause the key to the whole: the Father wishes to be acknowledged and worshipped in the Son, so our duty is to seek him in Christ and worship him in Christ; all men admit in the abstract that God should be worshipped, yet their minds lose themselves once they leave the appointed way. John Chrysostom presses the tribunal itself, since we shall render account of words as well as works; the man who has cast that day out of his soul runs like a horse that has burst its bridle towards a precipice.
24:
latin-fathers Gloss asks why a man should be told to hear the word of one and believe in another, and answers that the two are one act: to hear his word is to hear him, and to believe in the sender is to believe in his Word — that is, in the Son, who is the Word of the Father. grammatical-historical Ellicott makes the same point differently: the Son’s word is the revelation of the Father, so that whoever hears it believes not on him only but on him who sent him. Barnes fixes the sense of hearing, which is not the outward act but receiving a thing properly and obeying it — many hear the gospel outwardly who neither understand nor obey — and adds that there can be no faith in the sender without faith in the sent. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem distinguishes two senses of faith, of which this verse illustrates the first, the assent of the soul to a particular point; and he marvels that what the righteous of old gained by many years of well-pleasing, Jesus now bestows in a single hour, as he did on the robber.

What follows the believing is read as a present possession. Ellicott says the repeated verily introduces one of the deeper truths, that eternal life is not future only but already held in germ by the man brought into communion with its source; and that the verse gives the earlier whom he willeth no limit except human receptivity. He and Robertson both correct the rendering to doth not come into judgement, Robertson adding that the perfect tense marks a completed passage out of spiritual death into spiritual life, and warning that in this discourse Christ moves quickly between physical and spiritual life and death. wesleyan-arminian Clarke gives the transition a geography: the seed of this life is sown the moment a man believes, and to pass from death to life is to change one’s country, for death is the country where every Christless soul lives, and the man who does not know God lives a dying life, or a living death. Wesley, however, attaches a single clause of his own to the exemption from condemnation — unless, he says, the believer make shipwreck of the faith.

reformed Calvin reads the verse as the definition of the honour just demanded, so that no one may think it consists in outward performance or in frivolous ceremonies. The doctrine of the gospel is the sceptre by which Christ governs the subjects the Father has given him, and he asks no other honour than obedience to it. Nothing is more common, he adds, than a false profession of Christianity; but all the honour hypocrites pay him is the kiss by which Judas betrayed his Lord, and though they call him King a hundred times they strip him of his kingdom when they will not believe his gospel. Gill notes only who it is that swears, the Amen, the true and faithful witness.

puritan-evangelical Henry summarises the claim: our Lord is declaring his authority as the Messiah, referring first to the raising of those dead in sin by the power of the Spirit and then to the raising of the dead in their graves; and the office of judge of all men can be exercised only by one who has all knowledge and almighty power. Augustine of Hippo speaks of the difficulty of expounding such a passage at all: a great matter is treated by very small masters, and hearers take in not according to the bountifulness of the gushing fountain but according to their own capacity — yet he who, being great, became small for our sakes gives hope, and the matter works more fruitfully in their hearts than the preacher does in their ears.
25:
Whether the dead here are the buried or the spiritually dead is the question that divides this verse. grammatical-historical Ellicott argues for the spiritual throughout, on three grounds: and now is cannot describe the physical resurrection, nor be satisfied by the few restorations during the earthly ministry; the closing verb must mean the higher spiritual life, as in the whole context; and the clauses run parallel to those of the verse before, hearing answering to hearing, the word of Christ to the voice of the Son of God, eternal life to living. The world, he says, is a vast moral graveyard where men lie dead in sin. Robertson agrees flatly, distinguishing this from the future resurrection named a few verses later, and noting that Christ here gives himself the title Son of God. reformed Calvin says it is generally agreed that spiritual death is meant, and that those who refer the saying to Lazarus or to the widow’s son at Nain are refuted by what follows; Christ is first showing that we are all dead before he quickens us.

wesleyan-arminian Wesley takes the opposite view in one line, naming the daughter of Jairus, the widow’s son and Lazarus as those who heard the voice. Barnes will not choose: the words apply to the dead in sin and to those in their graves alike, since Scripture often describes two similar events in one set of terms — the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the world, or the return from Babylon and the coming of the Messiah. The hour comes under the preaching of the gospel as well as in the raising of the dead, and it now is, since sinners were being converted under that very ministry. Clarke lays out distinctions instead of deciding, setting three kinds of death — natural, the separation of body and soul; spiritual, the separation of God and the soul; eternal, the separation of both from God hereafter — against a threefold life answering to them.

Among the latin-fathers, Augustine puts the verse as an answer to a question a hearer might raise: the Father quickens whoever believes in him, but does the Son not quicken also? The saying settles it, and and now is is added so that we may know the hour will not be long in coming; for as in the future resurrection we shall be roused by hearing his voice, so it is now. Calvin draws a lesson from the manner of the saying: when the Son of God swears so often about our salvation we perceive how eagerly he desires our welfare, and how much it matters that faith in the gospel be deeply fixed — for the claim that his voice has such power of giving life has some appearance of being incredible, and he therefore confirms it with an oath. Gill notes that the repeated asseveration is still pressing the argument for his equality with the Father.

Lightfoot supplies the expectation the words met. The Jews looked for a resurrection of the dead at the coming of the Messiah, and with reason, though not in the sense in which it came; the vision of the dry bones and the prophet’s promise that the dead should live suggested some such thing, yet they groped exceedingly in the dark about it. He quotes two rabbinic sayings that come nearer the mark than the rest — one that the peoples of the earth do not live, which agrees well enough with the apostle’s word about being dead in trespasses and sins, and another that the dry bones are the sons of men in whom there is no moisture of the law.
26:
grammatical-historical Barnes begins from the title: God is called the living God in opposition to idols, and in himself means his life is derived from no other being; every creature holds life at second hand, but God is underived and always existed as he is. Ellicott draws the inference: giving life to others can only be done by one who has in himself an original source of life, which the Father has and the Son also has. Robertson adds a point of grammar: the particles as and so mark the fact of the possession, not its degree. reformed Calvin sees here why the voice has such efficacy: it would not pour out life if he had not in himself the source of it. God has life in himself not only because he alone lives by his own inherent power but because, containing its fullness, he communicates it to all; and because his majesty, being far removed, would otherwise resemble a hidden spring, it has been openly manifested in Christ, an open fountain set before us. Gill takes the life to be eternal life laid up in covenant for the chosen.

When the Son received it is disputed. wesleyan-arminian Wesley answers in five words: by eternal generation; the life so held is absolute and independent. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem guards the same doctrine: only the begetter knows the begotten and the begotten the begetter, and neither did he who begat suffer loss nor is anything lacking to him who was begotten. Ellicott divides the question by states: to the pre-existent Son the possession was natural, as being equal with the Father, while to the Son who had emptied himself of the exercise of those attributes it was part of the gift by which the Father exalted him — a gift in time to one who had it before all time. Clarke reaches the same result more briefly, taking the words as spoken in Christ’s character of envoy of God.

The second verse turns on a point of punctuation with a doctrine attached. eastern-antiochene Theophylact rejects the common reading, which joins because he is the Son of man to the grant of judicial power, since the connection has no meaning: Christ does not receive power to judge because he is man. Clarke follows him, adopting the punctuation of the Syriac and Armenian and of several Greek fathers, which carries the clause forward to the next verse. Against them, Ellicott insists the clause belongs where it stands and presses the missing articles: the phrase is a son of man, not the usual title of the Messiah, and stands in contrast to the Son of God above; it is not because he is Messiah but because he is human that this was given. Robertson renders it the same way, since the judge of men must partake of human nature. Wesley says plainly that he is appointed to judge mankind because he was made man.

Lightfoot supplies the prophetic background, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of days and receives dominion — a figure the rabbis identify with the King Messiah; and when Christ used that language before the council they at once asked whether he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed. Barnes describes what the authority must include: power to raise the dead and to investigate the actions and thoughts of a life, and the moral right to sit in judgement. Calvin takes the word for rule and government, the Father having appointed him King to govern the world with the Father’s own power, that he might impart what he has received. Theophylact explains why Christ dwells so constantly on judgement, resurrection and life: these are the likeliest arguments to prevail with obstinate hearers, since a man persuaded that he will rise and be called to account will be anxious to propitiate his Judge.
28:
reformed Gill offers three things the marvel might attach to — the cure of the man diseased thirty-eight years, the Son of God being also son of man, or, as he prefers, the dead hearing the voice of the Son of God and living upon it. wesleyan-arminian Clarke, having carried the previous clause forward, reads the sentence as beginning marvel not at this, because he is the Son of man, and refers it to the prophet’s vision of one coming with the clouds, which the Jews applied to the Messiah. grammatical-historical Ellicott takes it of the two things just claimed, that Christ has in himself a source of life and authority to judge. He notes that the coming hour is announced here without the earlier addition and now is, so that what is in view is the victory over physical death. Robertson marks the word for the graves, which is not the term suggesting burial but the one meaning a memorial; Christ here claims power to quicken the actually dead at the last day, a general bodily resurrection and judgement for good and bad alike. Barnes presses the extent: all the dead of every age and nation, and though many have long since turned to dust, God sees them and can regather them — though the phrase does not prove that the same particles of matter will be raised.

Calvin raises an objection against the argument itself. It may look as though Christ reasons inconclusively in confirming what he says by appeal to the last resurrection, since it is no greater exercise of power to raise bodies than minds. His answer is that the comparison is drawn not from the fact but from the opinion of men: being carnal, they admire nothing but what is outward, and pass by the resurrection of the soul with little concern while the resurrection of the body excites their wonder. The same stupidity, he adds, is why what is perceived by the eyes has more power to produce faith than what can be received by faith alone.

On the two issues of that hour they agree in substance. Gill says they shall come forth as Lazarus came forth at the word of command. Barnes explains the phrase resurrection of life: religion is often called life, and the righteous will be raised to the full enjoyment and perpetual security of it — the enjoyment of God, the society of angels and of the redeemed, freedom from sickness and sin and dying — and it bears that name because there shall be no more death. wesleyan-arminian Wesley compresses the same into a line, that it is the resurrection which leads to life everlasting. Robertson observes that neither phrase occurs elsewhere in the New Testament and that, the articles being absent, the sense is a resurrection of life and a resurrection of judgement: two resurrections as to result. Ellicott corrects damnation to judgement and notices that the words used here for practising and for evil are the only instances of either in this Gospel; the double opposition ties the verse to the earlier passage on light and darkness, so that the law of the spiritual resurrection now is the law of the resurrection hereafter.

Calvin guards the criterion from misuse. Christ points out believers by their good works, as elsewhere he teaches that a tree is known by its fruits. The robber to whom he promised life had been given up to crimes all his life and could only express a desire to do good with his latest breath; but since he was born again a new man, and from being the slave of sin began to be a servant of righteousness, the whole course of his past life was not reckoned before God. Nor are the sins on account of which believers daily make themselves liable to condemnation imputed to them.
30:
reformed Gill reads the verse as the winding up of the whole argument: Christ had been speaking of the Son as though of a third person, and now applies it all to himself — I am the Son who can do nothing separate from the Father, and to whom the Father shows all that he does. puritan-evangelical Henry says the same, that our Lord returns here to his declaration of the entire agreement between the Father and the Son, and so declares himself the Son of God. Robertson notes the grammatical mark of that return, since the discourse goes back to the first person after speaking of the Son since the earlier verse.

grammatical-historical Ellicott takes the verse as the thought with which the discourse opened, now applied to judgement: as in all his works, so in giving life and in judging, the Son cannot act apart from the Father, and the judgement must be just because it is not the sentence of an isolated will but one in accord with the eternal will of God. Robertson puts it more plainly: judges often have difficulty knowing what is law and what is right, but the Son’s task as judge is simple enough, being the will of the Father which he already knows. Barnes explains the verb: to hear expresses the condition of one commissioned or instructed, so that Christ represents himself as taught and sent, come to show men what God would have them know. wesleyan-arminian Wesley states the ground in a line, that it is impossible he should do anything separately from the Father because he is essentially united to him.

Lightfoot hears an allusion to a judicial custom of the day: when the judge of an inferior court was in doubt on any matter, he went up to Jerusalem, took the determination of the council, and gave sentence according to what he had heard. Among the latin-fathers, Augustine treats the words as anticipating an objection — will you then not judge according to the Father? — and answers that nothing departing from or unlike what the Father wishes will ever be seen done by him, since it is impossible that he should wish anything else; his meaning is that it is as if the Father judged. Augustine also observes the change of verb, that where the resurrection of the soul was in view Christ said see and here says hear, hearing implying a command from the Father; and this may be referred either to the human subordination of the Son of man or to the immutable nature.

Calvin refuses to follow the question that far. It would be superfluous, he says, to enter into abstruse reasonings about whether the Son hears so far as his eternal divinity is concerned, since Christ never meant to keep our minds employed on such trifles; and there was no reason for the ancients to give themselves so much anxiety in refuting the calumny of Arius, who argued from such words that the Son is not equal to the Father. Christ is not speaking of his divinity simply, but warning us that, so far as he is clothed with our flesh, we must not judge of him by the outward appearance. wesleyan-arminian Clarke turns the same point into a pattern: the human nature which is the temple of his divinity is perfectly subject to the deity dwelling in it, and in this our Lord is the model for all his followers, whose wills should in everything submit to their heavenly Father’s. Nothing is more common, he adds, than to hear a man say he will do a thing because he chooses; and he who has no better reason for his conduct than his own will shall in the end have the same reason to give for his destruction.
31:
The saying is a difficulty before it is a doctrine. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom asks it bluntly: does not Christ in many places bear witness of himself? And if all that is false, where is our hope of salvation, when Truth itself says that its witness is not true? His answer is that true here is said not of the intrinsic value of the testimony but of their suspicions, since the Jews might say they would not believe him because no man who witnesses to himself is to be depended on; and to meet that, Christ puts forward three irrefragable proofs, beginning with the works he had done. reformed Calvin says the same in his own idiom: Christ takes nothing from the credit due to his testimony, which he elsewhere asserts strongly, but speaks by way of concession — if my testimony about myself is suspect by the ordinary custom of men, let it go for nothing. It would be unjust to reduce the Son of God to that rank, yet he prefers to surrender his right in order to convince his enemies by the authority of God.

The legal background is agreed. Gill notes that no man was allowed to be a witness in his own cause, and that by the Jewish canon a man might not even witness for his wife, who was reckoned as himself. grammatical-historical Barnes recalls that the law required two witnesses, so that although what Jesus said was true he admitted it was not sufficient alone to claim their belief, and they had a right to expect confirmation. Robertson observes that the rule held in Jewish, Greek and Roman law alike, and points to the paradox that elsewhere Jesus insists his witness about himself is true, because the Father confirms it — the two required witnesses being Father and Son. Here he yields to the rabbinical demand for proof outside himself. Ellicott makes the verse the hinge of the chapter, the link between what has been said of Christ’s person and the witness about to be borne to him: he can do nothing of himself, and does not even bear witness of himself, since if he did it would on technical grounds not be credited.

puritan-evangelical Henry turns the concession into an indictment of the human race. Though the testimony is infallibly true, by the common rule of judgement among men it will not be admitted as legal proof; and that rule reflects reproach on the sons of men and their veracity, since we may say deliberately what the psalmist said in haste, that all men are liars — otherwise it would never have become a received maxim that a man’s testimony about himself is not to be relied on. wesleyan-arminian Wesley resolves the sentence by a parenthesis: if I alone testify, which indeed is impossible, my testimony is not valid. Clarke agrees that common sense would direct them to reject a claim with no proof behind it, but says the power of God by which the miracles were worked sufficiently attests it; and he reports a bishop’s proposal to render the words as a question — if I bear witness of myself, is my witness on that account not true?

John Chrysostom prefaces the passage with a warning about method. A man unpractised in the art who undertakes to work a mine will get no gold, but will confound everything aimlessly and undergo a labour unprofitable and pernicious; so those who do not understand the method of Holy Scripture, nor search out its peculiarities and laws, but go over all its points carelessly and in one manner, will mix the gold with earth and never find the treasure laid up in it. The passage before us, he says, contains much gold, not manifest to view but covered over with much obscurity, so that only by digging and purifying can the legitimate sense be reached.
32:
Who the other witness is divides the witnesses at once. grammatical-historical Ellicott, Robertson, Barnes and wesleyan-arminian Wesley all take it of the Father, Ellicott holding that the reference to the Baptist is excluded by the words that follow and that the whole point lies in the fact that another, different in personality from Christ himself, bears the witness. Robertson notes that the participle is a present, a continual witness of the Father resumed a few verses later. Clarke agrees and specifies how the Father witnesses: by his Spirit in the prophets he described the person, office and miracles of the Messiah, so that men who read those Scriptures cannot help seeing that they testify of Christ, no one else ever having answered the description. reformed Gill dissents. The Father is named particularly a few verses on, he says, and the thread of the discourse is a gradation — first another man, that is John, who is named by name in the very next verse; then a greater than he, the works; and only then the Father.

A textual variant sits in the same verse. Ellicott reports that two of the oldest manuscripts and some of the earliest versions read ye know for I know, a reading adopted by some modern editors, but he thinks its origin obvious and does not follow it. Clarke reports the same variant without deciding, and draws out what it would mean: you believe the Scriptures to be of God and that he cannot lie, and yet you will not believe in me though those Scriptures have so clearly described me. Wesley reads the received text as an appeal to their own standards, that even in their judgement this testimony is beyond exception.

On the deputation to John the witnesses converge. Gill observes that the council sent priests and Levites all the way from Jerusalem to beyond Jordan, and would never have been at such pains and charge unless they had held the man a faithful witness. Ellicott and Robertson both press the perfect tenses — ye have sent, he hath borne witness — which make the mission an official and permanent fact that the council is bound to recognise; and Ellicott sets the emphatic ye against the I of the following verse, since they sought human witness while he had witness that was divine. Barnes calls John eminent, candid, unambitious and sincere, his evidence impartial, and observes that many of the Pharisees had believed on him, so that Christ might have rested his whole proof here had he not been willing to adduce evidence of a higher order.

Clarke sets out four circumstances that make the testimony unexceptionable: John was consulted by Christ’s own enemies as a holy and extraordinary man; he was free of all self-interest, having declined to make the least advantage of his own reputation; he was so sincere and undaunted, and so averse from flattery, that he reproved a tetrarch at the hazard of his liberty and his life; and he was so far from having been solicited by Christ to testify that he had not even seen him when he did so. Calvin turns the argument into an accusation. Before producing the testimony of God, Christ presses them with the answer they had themselves obtained, from which they could not honourably withhold belief; for what use was there in sending, if they never meant to abide by what they were told? They received John as a prophet of God and pretended his word would count with them as an oracle — and Christ charges openly that nothing but their own malice keeps them from believing. Wesley states in six words what John had testified: that I am the Christ.
34:
reformed Gill says Christ stood in no need of human testimony and did not rest the truth of his deity and sonship on one, since the testimony of God is greater. wesleyan-arminian Clarke agrees he had no need of John, the works bearing sufficient testimony, but adds the argument to be made from it: you believed John a prophet, and a prophet cannot lie; he testified that I am the Lamb of God; therefore I appealed to his testimony that you may be saved by believing in me as such. grammatical-historical Ellicott refuses to soften the word: Christ did receive witness from men, and had received it from John, but that was never the witness on which everything rested — its purpose was to lead them to Christ himself. Robertson renders it as a refusal to take the witness simply from a man. Barnes adds a general observation: men are often dissatisfied with the very evidence they sought and professed themselves willing to rely on.

Calvin faces the apparent inconsistency. It was not in vain that God appointed witnesses to Christ; but he avails himself of John’s testimony not because he needs it, only so far as we profit by the confirmation. Men borrow from one another because they cannot dispense with the assistance; the case is different with God, for if the philosophers can say that virtue needs no foreign aid, what has man in himself to lend support to the truth of God? Wesley fixes on the closing purpose — so really and seriously did he will their salvation — and adds that they were not saved, and most of them died in their sins. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem applies the principle to his own preaching: unless you receive the testimony of the prophets on each matter, believe nothing I say; a teacher speaking now may reasonably be suspected, but what man of sense will suspect one who prophesied a thousand years beforehand?

The description of John turns on a word. Ellicott renders it the lamp that is lighted and then giveth light, insisting the change matters, since the prologue said expressly that John was not the Light but came to bear witness of it.
