Clarke translates the same way: John was not the light of the world, which is the sun, but a lamp giving clear and steady light until the sun should rise. Barnes notes the word is not the one used of the sun but of a light kindled artificially, and that a teacher is often so called because he illuminates other minds. Robertson distinguishes it from the torch fed with oil and quotes the verdict that when the Light comes the lamp is no longer needed. Lightfoot supplies the idiom, since that nation called any man famous for life or learning a candle, whence the rabbis were titled the candle of the law.

Why the tense is past they agree: Clarke, Barnes and Robertson all take it that John was by now in prison, his ministry over and his light no longer shining. Gill fills out both halves — he burned with love for Christ and for the souls of men, and his light of pure doctrine and holy conversation shone visibly — and Wesley compresses it: inwardly burning with love and zeal, outwardly shining in all holiness. Calvin makes the whole a reproach. Calling John a lamp proves their ingratitude, for they are blind only because they choose to be, God having kindled a light before their eyes that they should not go astray; their failure to acknowledge Christ is therefore voluntary error. Worse, they did not merely shut their eyes to it but abused it, being ready to applaud John beyond his deserts out of a treacherous design against Christ; and their willingness to rejoice in him lasted only for a season.
36:
reformed Gill begins with a mistranslation. The Latin and Ethiopic versions read greater than John, which is wrong: what is being compared with the works and with the Father’s testimony is not the man but his witness, so that the sense is a witness greater than John’s. Robertson renders the Greek the same way — literally, I have the witness greater than John’s — and observes that good as the Baptist’s testimony was, Christ has a superior one. wesleyan-arminian Clarke concedes everything that could be said for the lesser witness before setting it aside: however decisive the judgement of such a man as John, the lamp of Israel, a miracle of grace, filled with the spirit of Elijah and more than a prophet because he pointed out a Messiah already come, Christ is not obliged to depend on that testimony alone. And Clarke puts the natural question — how is it proved that God bears testimony to him? — and answers it from the works: miracles that nothing less than unlimited power and boundless love could produce, since by a word only he had instantly healed a man diseased thirty-eight years.

What the works are is less agreed. grammatical-historical Barnes takes them to be the miracles, the healing of the sick and the raising of the dead, and dwells instead on the verb: the works were committed to Christ to be performed until the task was complete, which is why he said at the last that it was finished, and why he so often guarded his life and sought safety until the work was done. Ellicott insists the term is wider. The parenthesis about John shows that John was not the other witness spoken of earlier, and this verse shows that the witness meant is that of the works — works which were not confined to what we call miracles but included the several parts of his messianic task, the doing of which was his food, and whose voice the hearers ought to have caught. Robertson adds a qualification of his own: Christ held that the highest form of faith does not require these works at all.

Calvin sets the verse in the argument. Having shown that the Jews had wickedly corrupted God’s gift in the person of John, Christ repeats a second time that he has no need of the testimony of man, as if he had not enough in himself; and perceiving that they held his person in contempt, he sends them, as his custom was, to his Father. Two things are held out to view as proving him the Son of God: that the Father attests it by miracles now, and that before he came into the world the Father had given abundant testimony to him in the sacred writings. And Calvin reminds us what the object of the whole is — that Christ wishes to be recognised as the Messiah promised by God, so that he may be heard. Ellicott makes the same point from the tenses, since the sending was at a definite moment while the witness went on continuously.
37:
When the Father bore this witness draws five answers. grammatical-historical Barnes lists three possibilities — the miracles, the voice at the baptism, and the Old Testament prophecies — and says it is not easy to decide, perhaps all three being meant. wesleyan-arminian Wesley chooses the baptism, and adds a sharp aside: he is not speaking of his supposed father Joseph, and they are utter strangers to the Father he means. Clarke answers by his prophets, and following a bishop makes the second half a parenthesis: not that the Father ever appeared visibly or spoke audibly to any of you, but that he did it through the prophets — though lately, he adds, a voice from heaven had been added. Ellicott rejects the appeal to the heavenly voices: the transfiguration was still future and the baptism would have required a more definite reference; the phrases his voice and his shape are general, and at any time stretches over the whole duration of previous revelation. Robertson goes furthest, denying that any audible voice is in view — not the baptism, not the mount, not the later voice many took for thunder — and referring the words to the Father’s witness in the believer’s heart, which comes neither by voice nor by form.

reformed Calvin agrees that limiting the statement to the baptism is a mistake, since the past tense shows Christ did not come forward as an unknown person, the Father having long ago distinguished him by marks he might bring with him. God testified concerning his Son whenever he held out to the ancient people the hope of salvation, so that they ought to have formed their idea of Christ from the prophets before he was manifested in the flesh.

Barnes counts the charges: they had not obeyed the command of God, had not regarded his manifestations either under the old dispensation or now, and did not yield to what he had said in the older revelation. Ellicott dwells on the image of a word taking up its abode in the mind and shaping the mind it dwells in, a thought found in this evangelist alone. They had the word of God but not as a power living in them; they locked it up with sacred care in ark and synagogue, but it found no home in their inmost life and they could take it up and put it down. Had it been in them it would have bred a consciousness that recognised every fuller revelation as of one nature with itself. Clarke says it more bluntly: they believed the Scriptures to be of God yet never let them take hold of their hearts, so the word was in their mouth but not in their mind — a miserable lot, to read the Scriptures as the true sayings of God and get no salvation from them.

Gill weighs three senses of his word: Christ himself, the Word made flesh; or, more probably, the written word and especially the prophecies of the Messiah; or the word spoken from heaven at the baptism, which left no lasting impression. Robertson notes that God’s word had come through the centuries by the prophets, and that the emphatic demonstratives set the rejected Son against the rejected Father. Calvin makes the failure the proof of the charge. This is the true way of profiting, when the word takes root in us and, impressed on the heart, keeps its fixed abode there; and Christ affirms the heavenly doctrine has no place among them precisely because they will not receive the Son on whom it everywhere bestows commendation. Moses had no other intention than to send all men straight to Christ, so that those who reject Christ are not the disciples of Moses. Wesley states the positive side: all who believe have the word of the Father abiding in them, deeply ingrafted in their hearts.
39:
Whether the opening word is a command or a description has been argued, grammatical-historical Ellicott says, through the whole history of New Testament exposition, with opinion among those best qualified to judge almost equally divided. It is not a question of the form of the Greek, which may be either, so that the English reader is in a position to form his own opinion and has almost all the evidence before him; but Ellicott points out that every parallel verb in the context is an indicative, and renders it ye search the Scriptures. Lightfoot had said the same, and wesleyan-arminian Clarke argues it at length: the imperative reading can never accord well with the verse that follows, and the force of the words is lost by it. Robertson agrees, resting the case on the reason that is given — because ye think — which is plainly indicative, and on the fact that Christ is arguing from their own use of the Scriptures. Wesley takes the other side flatly, calling it a plain command to all men. reformed Gill gives the imperative first and allows the indicative as an assertion; puritan-evangelical Henry offers both in turn, that they did search and did well to do so, and that the words may equally be an appeal — you profess to receive and believe the Scripture, let that be the judge.

The verb itself is strong. Barnes says it means to search diligently or anxiously, and collects the images it carries: it is used of miners looking for the bed of an ore with an intensity proportioned to their sense of its value, of a lioness robbed of her whelps tracing the footsteps of the man who took them, and of hounds tracking game by the scent. What it names is a diligent, faithful, anxious investigation. eastern-antiochene John Chrysostom makes the same point pastorally: if in the things of this life no great profit comes to a man who conducts his affairs in an indifferent and chance way, much more is this so in spiritual things; and Christ, referring them to the Scriptures, sent them not to a mere reading but to a careful and considerate search, since he did not say read but search.

That the searching was real is not in doubt. Gill notes that the oracles were committed to this people and read by them, not by kings and judges only but by common people who brought their children up to the reading of them, and that they were read and expounded publicly in the synagogues every sabbath. Clarke reports how strongly the rabbis recommended the study, quoting a passage in which God is brought in addressing David: I am better pleased with one day in which thou sittest and studiest the law than with a thousand sacrifices thy son Solomon shall offer on my altar. Perhaps, he adds, the Scriptures were never more diligently searched than at that very time. Robertson notes that the plural with the article points to the well-known collection, whereas elsewhere in this Gospel the singular means a particular passage.

What was wrong, then, was not the searching. Calvin says Christ does not absolutely blame them for seeking life in the Scriptures, since the Scriptures were given for that very end and use; he blames them because they supposed the writings gave life while they were themselves widely opposed to their natural meaning, and — what is worse — because they quenched the light contained in them. For how can the law bestow life without Christ, who alone gives life to it? They acknowledged the Scriptures and perceived in them nothing but the dead letter. Henry states the same in a sentence that has outlived its occasion: it is possible for men to be very studious in the letter of the Scriptures and yet strangers to their power.
40:
The refusal is traced to the will. grammatical-historical Ellicott says the hindrance is moral and not intellectual, and puts it as a contrast: they search because they think they have, whereas if they were willing to come they would really have. He widens it into a warning: dictionaries and grammars and commentaries are tools, but the precious ore lies in the mine and must be extracted by every man for himself. Barnes draws three conclusions: that life is to be had in Christ and no other; that we must come in the way appointed, as lost sinners willing to be saved by him alone; and that the reason sinners are not saved lies in the will. Robertson calls the clause the tragedy of the rejection of the Messiah by the Messianic race.

reformed Gill is careful about what coming means. It is not corporeal, for many came to Christ in that sense, some for the loaves, some to see the miracles, some to hear him and some to catch at what they could; nor is bare attendance on his ordinances the coming meant, since eternal life is not connected with that. What is intended is a coming by faith. Calvin makes the refusal an accusation: nothing but their own malice hinders them from partaking of the life offered in the Scriptures, and their ignorance is imputed to wickedness and obstinacy. Since he offered himself so graciously they must have been wilfully blind; and when they fled the light and desired to extinguish the sun by the darkness of their unbelief, he justly reproves them the more severely. wesleyan-arminian Clarke states the irony: though they search the Scriptures in hope of finding the Messiah and eternal life, they will not come to the one so clearly pointed out by them.

The disclaimer that follows is read as forestalling a suspicion. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom explains why it was needed: after the appeal to John, to the Father and to his own works, many who did not see his motive might suspect him of wanting human glory. His answer is that his nature is not such as to need the glory that comes from men — and if the sun receives no addition from the light of a candle, much less does he stand in need of human praise. Calvin adds the tactical reason: Christ declares that he does not care for glory and is not troubled to see himself despised, both because he is too great to depend on the opinions of men, whose whole malignity can take nothing from him, and so that he may not be suspected of pleading his own cause before pressing the charge that follows.

Gill guards the statement: honour is certainly due to Christ, and he does receive honour and blessing from his saints in their prayers and praises; what he denies is that in asserting his equality with the Father he was aiming at applause, or that in speaking of men coming to him he meant to gather a party and set himself up as a temporal king. Barnes takes the sentence as an explanation of their unbelief, and draws from it that human applause is of little value and often keeps men from the approbation of God. Clarke puts it directly: I do not stand in need of you or your testimony, and act neither through self-interest nor vanity; your salvation can add nothing to me, nor your destruction injure me, and I speak only through love for your souls. Ellicott prefers the rendering glory, and sketches the position of the men addressed: were they to follow this young Teacher, when they had schools of their own and disciples who held their teaching sacred and called them Rabbi? Robertson adds that the disclaimer is not wounded pride, ambition being no motive of Christ’s, who seeks the glory and fellowship of the Father.
42:
grammatical-historical Robertson notes the perfect tense — I have come to know and still know — and that the phrase means love toward God rather than God’s love toward them. reformed Gill says more briefly that being the omniscient God he knew not only their persons but their hearts. Ellicott turns the charge against their own profession. The principle that excludes the seeking of honour from men is the love of God; they claimed to be jealous for God’s honour, and the first precept of the law was that love, which every one of them professed and bound in holy texts round brow and arm, the Pharisees making broad the cases that held the words. They had them without and lacked the principle within, and there were marks in the heart which he read as plainly as the letters worn on the body. wesleyan-arminian Clarke puts the answer into Christ’s mouth: do not say you oppose me out of zeal for God’s honour, for I know your dispositions, and it is incorrigible ignorance and malicious jealousy that move you. Had you been as diligent to find the truth as to find allegories and false glosses, he adds, you would have known that the Messiah must be the Son of God. Calvin observes that love here stands for all religious feeling, since no one can love God without beholding him with admiration and submitting entirely to his authority, which is why the law was summed up in that command. Wesley catches the tone: with this ray he pierces the hearts of the hearers, and doubtless spoke with the tenderest compassion.

The contrast was a matter of ordinary custom. Clarke explains that among the rabbis it was essential to a teacher’s credit that he support his doctrine by the authority of some eminent man before him, whence the very form of coming in another’s name; and he takes the alternative for historical fact, since more than one impostor was afterwards received. Barnes describes the other sort of teacher as one setting up himself without even pretending to a divine commission, and remarks how accustomed that people were to follow particular masters. Robertson renders the clause and yet ye do not receive me.

Gill and Ellicott both press what coming in the Father’s name means. Gill says Christ came not of his own accord by a separate power and will, but was called and sent by mutual agreement, bringing his credentials in the works given him to finish. Ellicott says that so far from self-assertion he came as representing the Father, guided only by his will; had they loved the Father they must have received the Son, and the absence of love is at the root of the rejection. The true Israelite, he adds, became the true Christian; these were not true members of the old covenant and could not pass into the new. Calvin uses the verse as a test of teachers. False prophets boast of the same title, and under that disguise men have been deceived from the beginning; but Christ means the reality, since to come in the Father’s name is not only to be sent but faithfully to execute the commission received. By that mark lawful teachers are distinguished from the spurious, and we are taught boldly to reject all who in their own name claim authority over souls.

eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem reads the second half as fulfilled prophecy: by setting at nought the one who came and looking for one who comes in wickedness, they rejected the true Messiah and wait for the deceiver, being themselves deceived. He then turns a question on them: is the prophet who says that Emmanuel shall be born of a virgin true or false? If they charge him with falsehood it is no wonder, since their custom has been not only to charge the prophets but to stone them.
44:
The question is treated as a diagnosis rather than a taunt. grammatical-historical Ellicott puts the whole weight on the pronoun: it is not possible that ye should believe, because the two positions are entirely different — you receive glory from men and I do not, I have come in my Father’s name and you have not. They are in wholly distinct spheres of life and action and thought, so that to believe would mean giving up their whole present existence; and while they are what they are, it cannot be. Robertson agrees, and says they were not true Jews who cared for the glory of God but men who preferred the praise of men, like those who afterwards feared to confess Christ openly; he notes too that the best texts of the closing phrase vary, though the sense of the only God is certainly meant.

reformed Gill fills in the picture from their habits: they were ambitious of respect from one another and from the people, did all their works to be seen, chose the uppermost rooms at feasts and the chief seats in the synagogues, delighted in the pompous repetition of their title, and looked for a temporal kingdom in which they would be advanced to places of honour and profit — all of which stood in the way of believing in one who appeared in so abject a form. grammatical-historical Barnes says the same and generalises it: they were unwilling to renounce their worldly honours for one so humble and unostentatious, having expected a Messiah of pomp and splendour whom it would have been an honour to follow; and the great reason why multitudes do not believe is their attachment to human honours.

wesleyan-arminian Clarke states the cost exactly. The grand obstacle was pride, vanity and self-love, and they lived on each other’s praise; if they had acknowledged Christ as the only teacher they must have surrendered the good opinion of the multitude, and they chose rather to lose their souls than forfeit their reputation among men. This, he says, is the ruin of millions, who would be religious if religion and worldly honour were connected, but who will not accept salvation on the terms of self-denial, since the kingdom of Christ is not of this world. Wesley notices where the words fell: at the feast kept in commemoration of the giving of the law, their sermons used to be full of the praises of that law and of the people to whom it was given — and he asks how mortifying such a sentence must have been to men in the act of exulting in Moses.

Calvin answers the objection that the charge is too harsh. It might seem incredible that men trained from childhood in the law and the prophets should be convicted of such gross ignorance and declared enemies of the truth, and so Christ shows what it is that hinders them: ambition has deprived them of sound judgement. He is speaking in a peculiar manner to the priests and scribes, who, swelled with pride, could not obey God. Calvin calls it a remarkable passage, which teaches that the gate of faith is shut against all whose hearts are preoccupied with a vain desire of earthly glory; for the man who wishes to be somebody in the world has already made his choice.
45:
The disclaimer is read first as a refusal to imitate them. grammatical-historical Barnes says Christ will not follow their example, since it was they who had accused him, though he implies plainly enough that he might. wesleyan-arminian Clarke puts the retort in full: you accused me of breaking the sabbath, which I have shown false, and I could in return accuse you of breaking the whole law — but I need not, for Moses accuses you. He adds a maxim current among that people: none could accuse them but Moses. reformed Gill takes the denial absolutely: Christ is no accuser of men, not even of the worst; he came not to bring charges but to save, and the office suits none of his characters, of surety, saviour, advocate or judge — though there was enough to accuse these men of. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun and the force of the verb, which is to bring a public accusation in court.

Ellicott takes the question further back. Christ’s words had been direct accusation and must have cut to the quick, and since he had come from the Father it might have seemed to follow that he would accuse them there. Love cannot accuse, and he is a judge only because love must judge hatred and light must judge darkness by revealing it. And yet that revelation condemns them, so that the heart needs no accuser, for it accuses itself, and no sentence, for it condemns itself. Calvin draws a rule of pastoral practice: this is how we ought to deal with hardened persons when they learn nothing from instruction and friendly warning — they must be summoned to the judgement-seat of God. Few men openly mock him, but very many who believe that the God they oppose is gracious to them amuse themselves at their ease with empty flatteries.

Why Moses should be the accuser is variously put. Barnes and Wesley answer by his writings, since he foretold the Messiah and commanded them to hear him, so that they stand disobedient to a divinely commissioned lawgiver. Calvin makes the ground contempt of his doctrine, since no greater insult can be offered to the servants of God than that their teaching be despised; and God gave all his prophets a twofold commission, to teach for the salvation of believers and to confound the reprobate by their testimony. puritan-evangelical Henry widens the application: many trust in some form of doctrine, or in some party, who no more enter into its real meaning than these men did into the meaning of Moses. Let us search the Scriptures as men intent on finding eternal life, and observe how Christ is the great subject of them.

Where Moses wrote of Christ divides the last two. Clarke points to particular texts — the sceptre not departing from Judah until Shiloh come, and the promise of a prophet raised up from among their brethren — then adds that Moses pointed out the Messiah in a multitude of symbols found in the history of the patriarchs, in the ceremonial laws, and especially in the whole sacrificial system. Robertson agrees that the promise of a prophet was afterwards quoted as prophecy of Christ, and calls the sentence a home-thrust proving that they did not really believe Moses. Ellicott declines to confine the matter to particular passages: had they really believed Moses they would have seen in the whole spirit of the books a manifestation of God that must have led them to the fuller manifestation in Christ, for worship and sacrifice and priesthood were all meant to teach, and their own name for the law meant instruction. They accepted what the senses could know and never went beneath that surface, which is to say that they never believed Moses. Gill says it in a phrase: what was not believed was the doctrine of Moses.
47:
The chapter closes on an argument from the greater to the less. grammatical-historical Barnes states it plainly: if they do not credit what Moses wrote, which they profess to believe, it is not to be expected that they will believe Christ’s declarations. From that he draws four conclusions — that many who profess to believe the Bible have really no regard for it when it crosses their own views and inclinations; that it is our duty to study it, so as to be established in the belief that Jesus is the Messiah; that the prophecies of the older Scriptures are conclusive proofs of the truth of the Christian religion; and that he who rejects one part of the Bible will, for the same reason, reject the whole. wesleyan-arminian Clarke presses the same point on the men addressed: if they will not lay those writings to heart, or draw the conclusions which the letter as well as the spirit of them authorises, how shall they believe words against which they have taken up the most ungrounded prejudice? Until they see and acknowledge from the law and the prophets that the Messiah must have come, he says, they will never believe the gospel.

reformed Gill fixes exactly where the failure lay. They believed these to be the writings of Moses and to be the word of God; what they did not believe were the things contained in them concerning the Messiah, or rather they could not see that those things belonged and applied to Jesus of Nazareth — and therefore it was not to be supposed that they would credit him or his words. Robertson notes the contrast of terms, writings against words, and observes that the authority of Moses was for that people the greatest of all; he then surveys the range of the word rendered writings, which elsewhere can mean the bare letter as opposed to the spirit, a debtor’s bond, learning, official communications, or simply written characters, and which here names the sacred books.

Ellicott insists that the emphasis has been misplaced. The contrast is not between writings and words at all, but between his and mine: the verse repeats the thought of the one before it with an advance in time. They had not believed Moses, and therefore had not believed Christ; they do not believe now, because even now they do not read the spiritual meaning of what Moses wrote. What ground of hope is then left? Words revealing the deeper truths of the kingdom of God will fall on such ears as so many unmeaning sounds.

Calvin faces the difficulty the sentence raises. Christ appears here to claim less authority for himself than for Moses, and yet we know how much greater the gospel is; the answer is that he accommodates his discourse to those he is speaking to, since among the Jews the authority of the law was held sacred beyond all controversy, and it was in fact impossible that Christ should be inferior to Moses. The same contrast, Calvin adds, shows their unbelief to be the more aggravated, because the truth of God recorded in an authentic and acknowledged form still has no authority with them.
